clue.text: "What I would really like said about me is that I to love." (Maya Angelou) ()

definitions.text: "What I would really like said about me is that I to love." (Maya Angelou)

parts.words: "What I would really like said about me is that I to love." (Maya Angelou)
parts.note: a quotation with one word blanked out: the solver supplies the missing verb from Maya Angelou's line about having the courage to love

explanation.surface: A famous line from the American poet Maya Angelou with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation clue: the missing past-tense verb sits between 'I' and 'to love'. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelou wished to be remembered as someone who had the courage to risk loving; the missing past-tense verb means ventured boldly.

clue.text: English provincial lady of the French meadow

parts.note: in French 'of the' before a feminine noun is de la
a meadow is a grassy field

explanation.surface: An English country lady is introduced as hailing from a French meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: E. M. Delafield wrote 'Diary of a Provincial Lady', so the definition points at the author through her best-known book.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of the author of 'Diary of a Provincial Lady', a comic novel of English county life.

clue.text: Korzeniowski's wandering pet?

definitions.meaning: Joseph Conrad was born Józef Korzeniowski; one of his last novels has this title
a common name for a dog, and a word for someone who roams

explanation.walkthrough: Korzeniowski is Joseph Conrad's birth surname, so the first definition is a title of his. The question mark flags the pet as a typical dog's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad's 1923 novel bears this title, and it is also a stock dog's name meaning a wanderer.

clue.text: They may be frightened if you do it in the street, suggested Mrs Patrick Campbell

definitions.text: They may be frightened if you do it in the street, suggested Mrs Patrick Campbell

parts.words: They may be frightened if you do it in the street, suggested Mrs Patrick Campbell
parts.note: alludes to the actress's quip that people may do as they please so long as they don't do it in the street and scare the animals pulling the carriages

explanation.surface: A recollection of an Edwardian actress's remark on public misbehaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Patrick Campbell was a famous Edwardian stage actress; her line about not frightening certain animals in the street is the source.
explanation.definitionFit: In Mrs Campbell's quip, carriage animals are what public indecency would alarm, completing the phrase she made famous.

clue.text: In which Pope states "Most women have no characters at all"

definitions.text: In which Pope states "Most women have no characters at all"

parts.words: In which Pope states "Most women have no characters at all"
parts.note: asks for the title of the Alexander Pope epistle, addressed to Martha Blount, whose second couplet contains this line

explanation.surface: A notorious line from an eighteenth-century poet's verse letter about women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' is the poet Alexander Pope, not the pontiff: the line opens his Moral Essay II, an epistle addressed to a woman friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's second Moral Essay is titled as an address to a female friend, Martha Blount, and contains the quoted couplet.

clue.text: She finally got the pip

parts.note: 'the pip' looks like the slang for feeling irritated, but here it is Pip, the hero of Dickens's 'Great Expectations', whom the cold heroine ends up with

explanation.surface: A woman at last loses her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'get the pip' is British slang for becoming annoyed; read literally, it is Pip of 'Great Expectations', united with his beloved at the book's end.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Havisham's ward in 'Great Expectations', the girl Pip loves and is reunited with in the revised ending.

clue.text: Noblewoman of letters with elusive hero ()

definitions.text: Noblewoman of letters with elusive hero

parts.words: Noblewoman of letters with elusive hero
parts.note: a baroness who wrote novels, whose hero the French seek here and there and cannot find

explanation.surface: A titled lady author and her slippery protagonist.
explanation.walkthrough: The elusive hero is the Scarlet Pimpernel ('They seek him here, they seek him there'). The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroness Emma, Hungarian-born novelist, created the Scarlet Pimpernel, the uncatchable rescuer of French aristocrats.

clue.text: Multiple prizewinning dramatist, with complex plots

definitions.text: Multiple prizewinning dramatist, with complex plots

parts.words: Multiple prizewinning dramatist, with complex plots
parts.note: describes the Athenian tragedian who won the Dionysia festival contest many times and wrote intricately constructed tragedies

explanation.surface: A much-garlanded playwright known for intricate storylines.
explanation.walkthrough: The prizes are those of the Athenian drama festivals, where this tragedian is said to have won some twenty times.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek tragedian of 'Oedipus Rex' won first prize at Athens more often than any rival, and his plotting is famously tight.

clue.text: Once taken by leading families in Verona ()

definitions.text: Once taken by leading families in Verona

parts.words: Once taken by leading families in Verona
parts.note: the feuding Montagues and Capulets of 'Romeo and Juliet' each lined up against the other

explanation.surface: Something the great houses of Verona once took.
explanation.walkthrough: The families are Shakespeare's Montagues and Capulets; to 'take' these is to back one party in a quarrel. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposing factions in a feud; the two households of Verona each formed one party.

clue.text: Be fond of one's art, like cult US science fiction writer

parts.note: to be fond of something is to love it
one's art or skill is one's craft

explanation.surface: Advice to cherish your own creative skill, like a famous American fantasist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' is a link meaning 'such as' rather than a verb to be used in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: H. P. Lovecraft, author of the Cthulhu stories, is a cult figure of American weird and science fiction.

clue.text: Flying heart doctor

parts.note: looks like an airborne cardiologist; in fact the winged Roman god whose arrows deal with hearts

explanation.surface: A cardiologist on an air ambulance.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'doctor' tends hearts by striking them with love: the winged boy-god of Roman myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged Roman god of love, who flies about shooting arrows into hearts.

clue.text: Whither a funny thing happened in Shevelove and Gelbart's take on Plautus

definitions.text: Whither a funny thing happened in Shevelove and Gelbart's take on Plautus

parts.words: Whither a funny thing happened in Shevelove and Gelbart's take on Plautus
parts.note: the musical comedy by Burt Shevelove and Larry Gelbart, based on Plautus, is titled for a funny thing happening on the way to a Roman public square

explanation.surface: Where the comic incident in a Broadway version of Roman farce was headed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1962 musical 'A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the ...' adapts plays by the Roman comedian Plautus.
explanation.definitionFit: The public square of a Roman town, the destination named in the musical's title.

clue.text: Arthur Miller's boys in play

parts.note: the 1947 drama by the American playwright whose title speaks of all of a father's male children

explanation.surface: The playwright's sons fooling around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In play' looks like children at play but means 'as a play title': Miller's first Broadway success.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Miller's 1947 drama about Joe Keller is titled after all of a father's male offspring.

clue.text: The Terminator by Anthony Burgess

parts.note: a terminator is one who ends things, an ender
taken as written

explanation.surface: As if Burgess had penned the Schwarzenegger film.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: Burgess wrote a series of comic novels about the poet F. X. of that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of F. X., the flatulent poet hero of Burgess's 'Inside Mr Enderby' novels.

clue.text: Poet takes novelist on, we hear ()

indicators.note: signals that the words for novelist plus 'on', spoken, give a sound-alike

parts.note: the novelist Charles Dickens followed by 'on'

explanation.surface: A poet takes on a novelist, so it is rumoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes' is a link. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily of Amherst, the American lyric poet, bears this surname.

clue.text: All America follows divine messenger to prayers

indicators.note: the letters for the whole country come after those for the messenger

parts.note: an angel is a messenger of God
the US stands for all of America

explanation.surface: An entire nation trails a heavenly envoy to worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is a link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catholic devotion recited morning, noon and evening, commemorating the Annunciation, rung in by its bell.

clue.text: Lodge's run, running riot with weed

indicators.note: running wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the novelist David Lodge, with the s of the possessive kept as a letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A novelist's jog turns into a romp through the weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running riot' rearranges LODGESRUN; here the possessive s counts as a letter. 'With' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A common yellow-flowered garden weed of the daisy family.

clue.text: Greek lyric poet has a date in Rome with Mr Templar

parts.note: Simon Templar is the Saint, Leslie Charteris's gentleman adventurer
the Ides was a fixed date in the Roman calendar, mid-month

explanation.surface: A Greek poet goes on a Roman date with a fictional adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the date before the first name, but the pieces go in the answer as first name then date; 'has' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Simonides of Ceos, the sixth-century BC Greek poet of elegies and epitaphs.

clue.text: Like the office of Dr Swift

definitions.text: Like the office of Dr Swift

parts.words: Like the office of Dr Swift
parts.note: Jonathan Swift was Dean of St Patrick's in Dublin, so his office is described by the adjective from the Latin for dean

explanation.surface: A description of a quick physician's consulting room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dr' suggests a medic, but Swift was a Doctor of Divinity and Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relating to a dean, from Latin decanus; Swift held that church office in Dublin.

clue.text: Korzeniowski's wandering mate

parts.note: Conrad (born Korzeniowski) wrote of a disgraced ship's first officer who drifts from port to port

explanation.surface: A Polish-born author's roaming friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Korzeniowski is Joseph Conrad's birth name; 'mate' is a ship's officer, not a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad's 1900 novel follows a young ship's officer who abandons the Patna and wanders the East in shame.

clue.text: Blow reminiscent of Norah Lofts's climber, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to blow is an old word for to bloom or flower

definitions.text: reminiscent of Norah Lofts's climber, perhaps
definitions.meaning: Norah Lofts's novel title compares this verb to a climbing rose, so the word comes 'like the rose'

explanation.walkthrough: Norah Lofts was an English historical novelist; her 1939 book is 'Blossom Like the Rose'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bloom or flower; the first word of Lofts's title, which likens it to a climbing rose.

clue.text: Garb men change for Swedish playwright

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made to change places

explanation.surface: Instructions to swap outfits for a Scandinavian dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges GARBMEN; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingmar, the Swedish film and stage director, also wrote plays.

definitions.meaning: Angus Wilson's 1949 short-story collection is 'The ... Set'

explanation.walkthrough: Angus Wilson was a British novelist; the set is his story collection, not a group of people. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorrect; Wilson's collection title describes the social circle as unsuitable.

clue.text: Flower of Illyria (and something of a pansy) ()

definitions.meaning: the shipwrecked heroine of 'Twelfth Night', set in Illyria
a plant of the genus to which pansies belong

explanation.walkthrough: Illyria is the setting of Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night'. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's disguised heroine in Illyria, and the genus of violets that includes the garden pansy.

clue.text: Attack where Hitchcock felt most at home? ()

definitions.meaning: the start or assault of something, as of an illness

definitions.text: where Hitchcock felt most at home?
definitions.meaning: a film director is at work on the studio stage, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the second definition is the director's place of work on a film shoot. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: The beginning or assault of something; split, it is where a director works during filming.

clue.text: Seminal Jacobite security agent

parts.note: the Jacobites took their name from James II, the original king they backed
a bond is a security, a financial pledge

explanation.surface: A founding Jacobite turns out to be a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacobites supported the exiled James II and his heirs; 'seminal' marks the king their cause grew from.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's secret service spy, codename 007.

clue.text: Booth Tarkington's was from Indiana: Ivan Bunin's from San Francisco

definitions.text: Booth Tarkington's was from Indiana: Ivan Bunin's from San Francisco

parts.words: Booth Tarkington's was from Indiana: Ivan Bunin's from San Francisco
parts.note: two book titles share a noun: Tarkington's first novel and Bunin's famous story both name a well-bred man from a place

explanation.surface: Two authors' heroes and their home towns.
explanation.walkthrough: Booth Tarkington's 1899 novel and Ivan Bunin's 1915 story have titles of the same shape, naming a man of good breeding and his origin.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of good manners and standing, the title figure of both Tarkington's novel and Bunin's story.

clue.text: Income tax has made more of them out of Americans than golf, Will Rogers claimed ()

definitions.text: Income tax has made more of them out of Americans than golf, Will Rogers claimed

parts.words: Income tax has made more of them out of Americans than golf, Will Rogers claimed
parts.note: the American humorist joked that filling in tax returns turns more people into fibbers than golf does

explanation.surface: A humorist's quip about taxes and golf turning people dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: Will Rogers was an American cowboy humorist; golfers are proverbially dishonest about their scores. The empty brackets are a leftover of the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: People who tell untruths, as taxpayers do on returns and golfers do about scores.
